body.objective: Students will be able to identify my values.
successCriteria: I can identify my values and where they come from
I can explain how values guide decisions
I can discuss a dilemma respectfully
body.hook: You find a $20 bill on the hallway floor. Nobody saw you. What do you do? Most people answer quickly, but if you ask them why, the answers get interesting. Some say "because it's the rule," some say "because I'd want it back," and some say "because of the kind of person I want to be." Those reasons come from values.

vocabulary.definition: A belief about what is important or right.
Thinking carefully about what is right and wrong and why.
A situation where you must choose between options that each have good and bad points.
A rule or belief that guides behaviour, such as honesty.
A particular way of seeing a situation.

study.title: What Matters to Me?
study.question: What are my values, and how do they guide my choices?
study.passage:
Part 1, Values sort (10 minutes): Each student gets 20 value cards: honesty, kindness, fairness, loyalty, courage, responsibility, respect, family, friendship, freedom, achievement, faith or spirituality, creativity, health, fun, security, generosity, independence, justice, the environment. Sort them into "very important," "important" and "less important." Choose your top five.
Part 2, Where do values come from? (5 minutes): Families, cultures, faith communities, friends, teachers, experiences and media. Values can change as we grow.
Part 3, Values in action (15 minutes): Discuss these dilemmas in small groups. For each, name which values are in conflict.
A. Your best friend asks you to say they were with you on Saturday so they won't get in trouble at home. (loyalty vs honesty)
B. You see a classmate copying answers during a test. (fairness vs friendship)
C. Your team could win the championship if you play while slightly injured, against the coach's advice. (achievement vs health and responsibility)
Part 4, Discussion norms: Listen fully. Question ideas, not people. Give reasons. It's okay to change your mind.
There is not always one right answer, but some reasons are stronger than others.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Sort the value cards and choose your top five
Analyze three dilemmas for conflicting values
Reflect on how values guide your decisions
organizer: What I would do and why
discussion: Which of your top five values was hardest to choose?
In Dilemma A, which value would you choose, and why?
Did anyone in your group see a dilemma differently? How?
Can two good values conflict? Give an example.
study.product: Write a reflection on your top three values: where each comes from, a time it guided a decision, and a dilemma where two of your values might conflict.

examples.title: Conflicting values
examples.explore: How could you be both loyal and honest?

examples.title: Where values come from
examples.answer: Family, culture and experiences (also friends, faith, media)

examples.title: Reasons
examples.problem: Which is a stronger reason for returning the $20: "I might get caught" or "It belongs to someone"?
examples.answer: "It belongs to someone" reflects a principle of honesty
examples.explore: Why might principles be stronger reasons?

examples.title: Discussion norms
examples.problem: A classmate says, "That's a dumb opinion." What norm was broken?

practice.q: Why can two good values conflict?
practice.a: Situations can force a choice between things that both matter.

practice.q: Why are some reasons stronger than others?
practice.a: They rest on principles and consider others, not just self-interest.

practice.q: How can understanding others' values help in a disagreement?
practice.a: It shows why they see things differently and builds respect.

practice.q: In Dilemma A, describe an option that respects both loyalty and honesty.
practice.a: Sample: tell your friend you won't lie but will support them in being honest.
